draft.title: Sentencing in another state
card: Each Australian state and territory makes its own sentencing laws. The same offence can lead to different sanctions in different places.
Sanctions in every jurisdiction aim at the same purposes, such as punishment, deterrence, protecting the community and rehabilitation.
Comparing Victoria with another state shows different ways to meet those purposes. For example, a state may use a different type of order or set different limits on a sanction.
A comparison can show what works well in one place. It can also give reasons to reform the law in another.
draft.remember: Jurisdictions share sentencing purposes but may use different sanctions to meet them.

a.q: Why is it useful to compare Victoria's sentencing with that of another state?
opts: It shows other ways of meeting the same sentencing purposes
It shows that other states aim at different sentencing purposes
It shows that Victorian courts must follow that state's laws
It shows that one offence gets the same sanction everywhere
a.why: The purposes are shared, so a comparison shows different ways to reach them, which can suggest reform. The other options are wrong because each state makes its own laws, and outcomes can differ.
a.clue: Think about what stays the same and what differs between states.

b.q: A law reform group notes that another state uses a type of order that Victoria does not. The order aims to rehabilitate offenders. What does this comparison show?
opts: Another way to meet a purpose Victoria also pursues
Victorian courts must now adopt the other state's order
Victoria has no way to rehabilitate offenders at all
The other state has different purposes of sanctions
b.why: Rehabilitation is a shared purpose, and the other state meets it with a different tool. The comparison may support reform, but it does not bind Victoria. The tempting wrong option says the purposes differ, but they are shared.
b.clue: The purpose is the same. What differs is the method.

problems.detail: The clue ('The purpose is the same. What differs is the method.') states the answer outright. It rules out the 'different purposes' option and points straight to the correct one, so the question tests nothing.

The card says every jurisdiction aims at 'the same purposes', and why (a) and why (b) repeat this as absolute ('every jurisdiction', 'the same in every jurisdiction'). In fact the purposes are broadly similar but not identical. NSW's Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act s 3A also lists making the offender accountable and recognising the harm done to the victim and community. 'Broadly similar purposes' would be accurate.
